topics.title: SI prefixes and engineering notation
topics.summary: Read and use k, M, m, µ, n, and p, so that values like 4.7 kΩ and 10 µF go straight into formulas.

prerequisiteNotes.ohms_law: Every calculation here is Ohm's law with prefixed values: mA × kΩ = V.
prerequisiteNotes.power_heat: P = V·I, V²/R, and I²R, along with E = P·t, are the formulas the prefixes go into.

lensNotes.math: Engineering notation keeps exponents in steps of three, so every value is a number from 1 to 999 with a prefix. Multiplying prefixes is adding exponents: kΩ × mA = 10³ × 10⁻³ = volts, and kΩ × µF = 10³ × 10⁻⁶ = milliseconds.

goals: Convert a value between prefixes, for example 4700 pF = 4.7 nF and 0.1 µF = 100 nF
Put values like 4.7 kΩ and 2.2 mA straight into Ohm's law and power formulas, and give the result with the right prefix
Compare values written with different prefixes and say which is larger
Check the size of an answer before trusting it, and spot a lost k or m (an error of a factor of 1000)
topics.intuition: Each prefix step is a factor of 1000, so the prefix tells you a value's size at a glance. Multiplying two prefixed values adds their exponents, and dividing subtracts them: kΩ × mA gives volts, and V ÷ kΩ gives mA.
topics.why: Circuit quantities span an enormous range: a leakage current of a few nanoamps and a motor current of a few amps differ by a factor of a billion. Prefixes change none of the physics; they are powers of ten written in front of a unit. The laws themselves hold in base units: one ohm is one volt per amp, one volt times one amp is one watt, and one watt is one joule per second. So V = I·R is exact in volts, amps, and ohms, and prefixes only have to be carried through the arithmetic correctly.
topics.explanation: You already use prefixes outside electronics: a kilometer is a thousand meters, a millimeter is a thousandth of one. Electronics uses the same idea in steps of a thousand. Going up: k (kilo, 10³), M (mega, 10⁶), G (giga, 10⁹). Going down: m (milli, 10⁻³), µ (micro, 10⁻⁶), n (nano, 10⁻⁹), p (pico, 10⁻¹²). Engineering notation picks the prefix that leaves a number from 1 to 999, so 0.0047 A is written 4.7 mA. Formulas such as Ohm's law, V = I·R, and power, P = V·I, work in base units: volts, amps, ohms, watts. You can always convert everything first, but it is faster to combine the prefixes: milli times kilo is 10⁻³ × 10³ = 1, so mA × kΩ gives volts, and volts ÷ kΩ gives mA. Squaring squares the prefix too: (2 mA)² is 4 × 10⁻⁶ A², not 4 × 10⁻³ A². The same value can be marked several ways: 0.1 µF, 100 nF, and 100 000 pF are one capacitor. Before trusting a result, check its size. A few volts across a few kilohms should give a few milliamps; an answer in amps means a prefix was lost.

workedExample.problem: A 9 V battery is connected across a 4.7 kΩ resistor. Find the current, the power the resistor dissipates, and the energy it turns into heat in one hour.
steps: Convert to base units: 4.7 kΩ = 4.7 × 10³ Ω = 4700 Ω.
Current: I = V / R = 9 V / 4700 Ω = 0.001915 A = 1.915 × 10⁻³ A = 1.91 mA. Shortcut: volts ÷ kΩ gives mA, so 9 V / 4.7 kΩ = 1.91 mA directly.
Size check: a few volts across a few kilohms gives a few milliamps, so 1.91 mA is plausible. 1.91 A would mean the k was dropped.
Power: P = V × I = 9 V × 1.915 mA = 17.2 mW (volts × mA gives mW). Cross-check: P = V² / R = (9 V)² / 4700 Ω = 81 V² / 4700 Ω = 0.0172 W = 17.2 mW.
Energy: a watt is a joule per second, and one hour is 3600 s, so E = P × t = 0.01723 W × 3600 s = 62.0 J.
A common 0.25 W (250 mW) resistor is dissipating about 7% of its rating, so it runs only slightly warm.

templates.prompt: A current of {I} flows through a {R} resistor. What is the voltage across the resistor?
templates.explanation: Ohm's law: V = I·R = {I} × {R} = {answer}. Shortcut: mA × kΩ gives volts directly, because 10⁻³ × 10³ = 1.
hints: Which law links voltage, current, and resistance?
Use V = I·R with both values in base units (amps and ohms), or use the shortcut mA × kΩ = V.

misconceptions.feedback: You divided. Ohm's law is V = I·R: more resistance needs more voltage to push the same current.
R/I isn't a voltage. Ohm's law is V = I·R.

followUps.prompt: Why does multiplying milliamps by kilohms give plain volts?

choices.text: The prefixes cancel: milli is 10⁻³, kilo is 10³, and 10⁻³ × 10³ = 1
choices.feedback: Right: multiplying prefixes adds their exponents, −3 + 3 = 0, which leaves plain volts.

choices.text: Milliamps and kilohms are both "small" units, so they match
choices.feedback: Kilo is big (×1000) and milli is small (÷1000). They cancel because they are opposites.

choices.text: Ohm's law only works in mA and kΩ
choices.feedback: Ohm's law works in any consistent units; amps and ohms always work. mA and kΩ just happen to cancel.

choices.text: It doesn't: you must always convert to amps and ohms first
choices.feedback: Converting always works, but here it isn't needed: 1 mA × 1 kΩ = 10⁻³ A × 10³ Ω = 1 V.

followUps.explanation: Engineering notation steps in powers of a thousand, so multiplying prefixes means adding exponents in threes. mA × kΩ = 10⁻³ × 10³ = 10⁰, plain volts. The same idea gives V / kΩ = mA and kΩ × µF = ms. With ohms instead of kilohms, mA × Ω gives mV.

templates.prompt: A {V} source is connected across a {R} resistor. How much current flows?
templates.explanation: I = V / R = {V} / {R} = {answer}. Shortcut: V / kΩ gives mA.
hints: I = V / R. Convert {R} to ohms first, or remember that volts divided by kΩ gives mA.

misconceptions.feedback: That's R/V, upside down. Current is I = V / R: a bigger resistor lets less current through.
You multiplied. Current is I = V / R, so a bigger resistor means less current.

templates.prompt: A {V} supply is connected across a {R} resistor. How much power does the resistor dissipate?
templates.explanation: P = V² / R = ({V})² / {R} = {answer}. Check: I = V / R = {I}, and P = V·I gives the same result.
hints: Power in a resistor can be written with V and R only.
P = V·I and I = V / R, so P = V² / R. Square the voltage first.

misconceptions.feedback: That's the current (I = V / R), not the power. Power is P = V·I = V² / R.
Power isn't V·R. Use P = V² / R: a bigger resistor draws less current and dissipates less power.
You multiplied by R. Use P = V² / R: divide the squared voltage by the resistance.

followUps.prompt: Why does the power depend on the voltage squared, not just on the voltage?

choices.text: More voltage also pushes more current (I = V / R), and power is voltage times current, so both factors grow
choices.feedback: Right: double V and you double I too, so P = V·I goes up four times.

choices.text: The square is just part of the formula; there's no physical reason
choices.feedback: There is a reason: P = V·I, and the current itself is V / R. One V from each factor makes V².

choices.text: The resistance rises as the voltage rises
choices.feedback: An ideal resistor keeps its value. The square comes from V·I with I = V / R, not from R changing.

choices.text: Power is energy, and energy always goes as a square
choices.feedback: Not always: E = P·t grows in step with time. The square here comes from V·I, with I rising in step with V.

followUps.explanation: P = V·I. In a resistor I = V / R, so P = V·(V / R) = V² / R. Doubling the voltage doubles the current, and their product goes up four times. That's why a modest overvoltage can overheat a resistor.

templates.prompt: A current of {I} flows through a {R} resistor. How much power does it dissipate?
templates.explanation: P = I²·R = ({I})² × {R} = {answer}. Square the current in amps first: milliamps squared are millionths.
hints: Power in a resistor can be written with the current alone.
P = I²·R, with I in amps.

misconceptions.feedback: That's I·R, a voltage. Power is I²·R (or V·I).
Square the current, not the resistance: P = I²·R.

templates.prompt: A {P} heater runs for {t}. How much energy does it use, in joules?
templates.explanation: Energy is power × time: E = {P} × {t} = {answer}. A watt is one joule per second.
hints: A watt is a joule per second.
E = P·t with t in seconds.

misconceptions.feedback: Dividing gives J/s², which isn't an energy. Multiply: E = P·t.

templates.noDrawing: energy from power and time for an appliance; no circuit is described

templates.prompt: The supply across a resistor of {R} is raised from {V} to {new_V}. What happens to the power the resistor dissipates?

feedback.down: The resistor hasn't changed, so more voltage pushes more current through it (I = V / R). More voltage and more current can only mean more power.
feedback.same: Power is V·I, and both rise with the supply. Only the resistance stays the same.

templates.explanation: P = V² / R: {before} → {after}. Doubling V also doubles the current (Ohm's law, I = V / R), so the power, V × I, goes up four times, not two.
hints: Does the current change when the voltage doubles?

templates.prompt: A resistor of {R} sits across a supply of {V}. A classmate works out the current and gets {Ibad}. Before redoing the sum, what is your verdict?

choices.text: About a thousand times too big: volts across kilohms give milliamps, so it should be about {I}
choices.feedback: Right: they most likely typed the resistance without its k. Volts ÷ kΩ = mA.

choices.text: About right: a few volts across a resistor gives around an amp
choices.feedback: An amp from a few volts needs a resistance of a few ohms. Across thousands of ohms, a few volts push only milliamps.

choices.text: About a thousand times too small: the k means the current should be multiplied by a thousand, to about {Ibig}
choices.feedback: The k multiplies the resistance by a thousand, which divides the current by a thousand. The true current is smaller, not bigger.

choices.text: The method is wrong: the current is the voltage times the resistance
choices.feedback: V × R isn't a current. I = V / R: more resistance means less current.

templates.explanation: Check the size before trusting a calculator. {V} / {R} = {I}. A result near amps means the k was lost: dividing by the bare number gives {Ibad}. Rule of thumb: volts ÷ kΩ = mA.
hints: Roughly how much current do a few volts push through a few thousand ohms?

templates.prompt: Four capacitors are marked {Au} µF, {Bn} nF, {Cp} pF, and {Du} µF. Which has the largest capacitance?

choices.text: {Bn} nF
choices.feedback: Right: {Bn} nF = {Bu} µF, more than {Au} µF, {Du} µF, or {Cp} pF ({Cn} nF). Put every value in one prefix before comparing.

choices.text: {Au} µF
choices.feedback: The µF prefix is the bigger one, but {Au} µF = {An} nF, less than {Bn} nF. The prefix alone doesn't decide: convert to one prefix before comparing.

choices.text: {Cp} pF
choices.feedback: It has the biggest number but the smallest prefix: {Cp} pF = {Cn} nF, against {Bn} nF.

choices.text: {Du} µF
choices.feedback: {Du} µF = {Dn} nF, less than {Bn} nF. A bigger prefix with a small number can still be the smaller value: put all four in nanofarads first.

templates.explanation: In nanofarads: {Au} µF = {An} nF, {Bn} nF stays {Bn} nF, {Cp} pF = {Cn} nF, and {Du} µF = {Dn} nF. Each prefix step is a factor of 1000, so a big number with a small prefix can be the smallest value. Parts are marked all these ways: 0.1 µF and 100 nF are the same capacitor.
templates.noDrawing: comparing capacitor markings in different prefixes; no circuit

templates.prompt: A push button pulls a microcontroller input to ground, and a pull-up resistor from the {V} rail holds the pin high while the button is open. With the button pressed, the resistor should draw about {I} from the rail (within 30%, so between {Ilo} and {Ihi}). Take the pin itself as drawing no current. Choose R from the E12 series, between 1 kΩ and 1 MΩ.
templates.explanation: When pressed, the button ties the pin to ground, so the whole {V} sits across R and I = V/R. Solve for R: R = {V} / {I} = {Rex}. Keep the prefixes straight: volts divided by milliamps give kilohms, and volts divided by microamps give megohms. Any E12 value from {Rlo} to {Rhi} keeps the current in range; pick one and check V/R.
hints: With the button pressed, what voltage is across the resistor?
R = V/I. Volts ÷ mA = kΩ; volts ÷ µA = MΩ.

followUps.prompt: A classmate works out 3.3 V ÷ 100 µA and gets 33 Ω. What went wrong?

choices.text: They used 10⁻³ for µ (the milli factor), so the answer is 1000 times too small: 3.3 V / (100 × 10⁻⁶ A) = 33 kΩ
choices.feedback: Right: µ is 10⁻⁶. Dividing by it multiplies by 10⁶, so V/µA comes out in MΩ: 3.3/100 MΩ = 33 kΩ.

choices.text: They should have got 330 Ω, because 100 µA is 0.01 A
Nothing: 33 Ω is right, a pull-up only needs to be small
choices.feedback: 33 Ω from 3.3 V draws 100 mA with the button pressed, a thousand times the target.

choices.text: They forgot to square the current
choices.feedback: Ohm's law is linear, R = V/I. The error is a factor of 1000, exactly one prefix step.

followUps.explanation: Dividing subtracts exponents: V / µA = 10⁰ / 10⁻⁶ = 10⁶, so the result is in MΩ. The same rule gives V / mA = kΩ. A current of a few microamps from a few volts therefore needs about a megohm, and a few milliamps about a kilohm.
